title: BofA Sees the End of ‘Easy Money’ Made From the AI-Spending Trade
source_used: Bloomberg News text on AdvisorHub (author field 'Bloomberg News'); Briefs Finance gives a short rewrite. Bloomberg original not opened (HTTP 403).
key_facts: Bank of America strategists led by Savita Subramanian wrote in a Monday (5 Oct 2026) note that investors will find it harder to make 'easy money' betting on AI-linked capital spending versus consumer-driven spending.
AI spending and shrinking discretionary spending (linked to white-collar job losses) are already baked into investment positions.

Positioning in 'AI disruptees' (information-technology services, consumer finance, software) in long-only active funds is near record lows; positioning in industrials is near record highs relative to consumer discretionary.
Over 12 months the S&P 500 Consumer Staples Index rose 4.6% while a consumer discretionary gauge fell 3.3%; Lululemon and Nike are each down about 50%.
Subramanian called the current positioning 'justified' since a shift from consumption to capex was a core thesis this year; BofA's November outlook favoured 'capex over consumption'.
Last week BofA said investors might want to 'get bulled up' as market risks had shifted to the upside.
quote_evidence: Investors are likely to find it increasingly hard to make “easy money” by betting on outsized returns from artificial intelligence-linked capital expenditures compared with consumer-driven spending, according to strategists at Bank of America Corp.
Subramanian said the current positioning is “justified,” as a likely shift to capex from consumption had been a core investment thesis for this year.
However, the S&P 500 Consumer Staples Index has climbed 4.6% in the period, while a gauge of the consumer discretionary stocks has fallen 3.3%.
why_it_matters_hint: A large US bank's strategists say the AI-spending bet is crowded and investors may need to rotate selectively.
